entries.question: Who appeared to Moses in the burning bush?
entries.summary: Exodus 3:2 says "the angel of the LORD" appeared to Moses in the flame, and Acts 7:35 confirms it was an angel. But Exodus 3:4 in the same passage shifts and says "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush," and Mark 12:26 has Jesus himself affirm that God spoke to Moses at the bush. Same encounter, two different speakers.
entries.commentary: The traditional solution — endorsed by Calvin, carried by Kaiser, Walton, and Stuart — is that "the angel of Yahweh" is a functional stand-in for Yahweh himself throughout the Hebrew Bible, so "angel" and "God" can name the same being without contradiction. Some apologists go further and read the angel as a pre-incarnate Christophany. The pre-incarnate-Christ reading is a dogmatic overlay, not anything the text suggests. But even the broader "angel as God-surrogate" claim is doing heavy lifting. Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have mapped the mal'akh YHWH formula across Hebrew Bible texts and shown it functions inconsistently — sometimes as Yahweh himself in disguise (Gen 16, Gen 22), sometimes as a genuinely separate emissary (Num 22, 2 Sam 24). In Exodus 3 the narrative oscillates: verse 2 has the angel appearing in the flame, verse 4 has Yahweh and Elohim both speaking. Friedman's source analysis splits the passage between J and E, each using different terms for the divine speaker. Carr, Baden, and Propp all treat the angel/God alternation in Exodus 3 as a redactor's seam rather than a unified theology — the E source tends to use "angel" or "God" circumlocutions while J uses "Yahweh" directly. The harmonization works at the level of mature second-temple theology (where "angel of Yahweh" got systematized as an avatar doctrine), but the Exodus 3 text itself preserves two source-strands with different names for who showed up at the bush.

entries.question: What is God's name?
entries.summary: The Hebrew Bible gives God several different "names" and in some cases insists that a particular one is THE name. Exodus 6:3 says God's name is Jehovah (YHWH), Exodus 3:14 gives "I AM THAT I AM," Isaiah 42:8 flatly claims "the LORD" is his name, Exodus 34:14 says his name is Jealous, Amos 5:27 says his name is the God of hosts, and Psalm 68:4 says his name is JAH. The contradiction is that multiple passages each claim to be stating THE divine name, and the names don't match.
entries.commentary: The apologist move here is predictable — these aren't different names, they're different titles or epithets for the same deity, like calling someone "Dad," "Mr. Smith," and "Bob" depending on context. Archer runs this line in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Kaiser does the same thing. Fine. That harmonization partially works for the epithets. "Lord of hosts" (YHWH tseva'ot) is clearly a title describing YHWH's military role, and "I AM THAT I AM" (ehyeh asher ehyeh) is widely read as a folk-etymology explaining the tetragrammaton. But the harmonization collapses on Exodus 6:3, which is the structural load-bearing verse in the Priestly source. P is doing something specific here: he's claiming YHWH was NOT known by that name to the patriarchs. That is flatly incompatible with the J source in Genesis, where YHWH is invoked by name as early as Genesis 4:26 ("then began men to call upon the name of the LORD") and where Abraham builds altars to YHWH in Genesis 12:8. This is one of the foundational data points for the Documentary Hypothesis — Friedman covers it at length in Who Wrote the Bible and The Bible with Sources Revealed. The J source uses YHWH from the beginning. The E and P sources use Elohim or El Shaddai until Exodus 3 (E) or Exodus 6 (P), where the name is revealed for the first time. So "what is God's name" has a real answer from critical scholarship: different sources had different theologies about when and how the divine name was revealed, and the redactor stitched them together without smoothing out the contradiction. The apologist "multiple titles" move doesn't touch that.

entries.question: Was Moses a good speaker?
entries.summary: Exodus 4:10 has Moses himself telling YHWH he is not eloquent and is "slow of speech, and of a slow tongue" — the whole reason Aaron gets attached to the mission. Acts 7:22, by contrast, has Stephen claiming Moses was "mighty in words and in deeds." The two verses assign Moses opposite verbal abilities.
entries.commentary: Apologists have a standard three-move playbook here. Archer runs all three. Move one: Moses was just being humble or suffering a confidence crisis in Exodus 4, not making a factual claim about his oratorical ability. Move two: Stephen is describing the young, Egyptian-trained Moses, while Exodus 4 is describing the older, self-doubting, forty-years-shepherding-sheep Moses. Move three: "mighty in words" means powerful in content, not fluent in delivery — so the two can both be true. These are not zero moves. Move two has genuine narrative texture to it — there IS a forty-year gap. But here's what the apologist has to do to make this work: reject Moses' own self-report as unreliable, accept Stephen's summary (delivered in a hostile trial setting, in Acts, a text written ~80 years after Paul by Luke, who is retelling a speech he did not witness) as the accurate biographical data, and then paper over the fact that YHWH doesn't respond to Moses in Exodus 4 by saying "no, you're actually a great speaker, I know your past." YHWH's response is to provide Aaron as a mouthpiece (Exod 4:14-16). The narrative itself treats Moses' speech impediment as a real limitation, not a confidence problem. Stephen's speech, on the other hand, is doing something different — it's a sweeping rhetorical summary of Israelite history designed to condemn his accusers, and it lionizes Moses for rhetorical effect. Luke is not writing biography; he's writing theological history. Pervo and Haenchen both treat Stephen's speech as a Lukan composition, not a verbatim transcript. So the contradiction is real at the level of the narrator's framing: one tradition has Moses as verbally inadequate (a detail the E-source narrator uses to elevate Aaron), the other has him as a rhetorical powerhouse (a detail that serves Stephen's argument). You can harmonize these if you work for it. You can't harmonize them cleanly.

entries.question: Who hardened the Pharaoh's heart?
entries.summary: Exodus gives contradictory agency for Pharaoh's heart. In Exod 4:21, 7:3, 9:12, 10:1, 10:20, 10:27, 11:10, 14:4, 14:8, and 14:18 YHWH explicitly hardens Pharaoh's heart. In Exod 8:15, 8:32, and 9:34 Pharaoh hardens his own heart. 1 Samuel 6:6 looking back attributes the hardening to Pharaoh and the Egyptians. The contradiction is over who is morally responsible for the hardening that triggers the plagues — God or Pharaoh.
entries.commentary: The standard apologist harmonization here is from Archer, Kaiser, and Stuart in his NAC on Exodus: Pharaoh hardens his own heart first (chapters 7-8), and God only ratifies or intensifies that hardening later (chapters 9-14). On this reading, Pharaoh is morally responsible because he initiates the hardening, and God's hardening is judicial — the Romans 1:24-26 "God gives them over" pattern. That is a clever reading and it picks up on a real narrative progression. The plain text does have self-hardening appearing in the early plagues and divine hardening concentrated later. But here's where it breaks down. Exodus 4:21 and 7:3 — BEFORE Pharaoh has done a single thing — already have YHWH declaring "I will harden his heart" and "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." This is programmatic, announced from the outset, and framed as the whole point of the plague sequence ("that I might shew these my signs before him," 10:1). Fretheim reads this correctly in his Interpretation commentary: the divine hardening is not a late-sequence judicial response; it's the theological engine that drives the whole narrative, because YHWH wants maximum display of power against the Egyptian gods. Source-critical scholars (Baden, Propp) note that the hardening vocabulary actually differs between sources — the P source uses חזק (strengthen), J uses כבד (make heavy), E uses קשה (make hard) — and the blending produces the inconsistency we see. So the apologist harmonization can squint and read a chronological escalation, but it has to ignore that the hardening is divinely pre-announced and theologically pre-committed. You can call that "God hardening Pharaoh who was going to harden himself anyway," but that's Calvinist compatibilism, not textual harmony. The text itself contradicts itself on the agency of the hardening.

entries.question: Did Abraham know God's name?
entries.summary: Genesis 22:14 has Abraham naming a place "Jehovahjireh" (YHWH-yir'eh, "YHWH will provide") — he knows and uses the name YHWH. Exodus 6:3 has YHWH telling Moses that he appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai (God Almighty), "but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them." The two verses are flatly incompatible.
entries.commentary: This is the cleanest single-verse contradiction in the Hebrew Bible, and it's a structural load-bearing verse in the case for the Documentary Hypothesis. The apologist moves are exhausting but they exist. Archer and Kaiser claim Exodus 6:3 doesn't mean the patriarchs didn't know the name YHWH, it means they didn't know the full meaning or full character represented by the name — a kind of "experiential knowing" versus "propositional knowing" distinction. Motyer tried this move too. That is an enormous amount of theological freight to hang on a single verb. The niphal of yada (to be known) in Exodus 6:3 is contrastive with "I appeared... by the name of God Almighty" — the syntax is specifically naming one name that WAS known and another name that WAS NOT known. The plain reading is that the name YHWH itself was not revealed before Moses. Kugel lays this out in How to Read the Bible: Genesis is riddled with uses of YHWH by the patriarchs (Gen 12:8, 13:4, 15:7, 22:14, 26:25, 28:13), and Exodus 6:3 has YHWH declaring that his name wasn't known to them. Friedman in Who Wrote the Bible identifies this as one of the fingerprints of source division — J uses YHWH from Genesis 4:26 onward, while P (Exodus 6:3) and E (Exodus 3:14-15) both treat the name as a Mosaic revelation. This isn't a contradiction that the apologist "experiential knowing" dodge can paper over, because the verses aren't saying "Abraham didn't grok YHWH's character," they're saying Abraham did and didn't know the name itself. Two authors with two different theologies of how the divine name entered history got stitched together. That's the parsimonious reading.

entries.question: Who was Libni's father?
entries.summary: Three Levitical genealogies in Exodus 6:17, Numbers 3:18, and 1 Chronicles 6:17 list Libni as a son of Gershon (Levi's firstborn). But 1 Chronicles 6:29, tracing a completely different Levitical line, has Libni as son of Mahli and grandson of Merari (Levi's third son). Same name, two different fathers, two different Levitical branches.
entries.commentary: The apologist move here is cheap and it sometimes actually works: two different men named Libni. Archer goes for this in Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Keil-Delitzsch did it before him. Harmonizers point out that Hebrew genealogies reuse names constantly — there are multiple Zechariahs, multiple Azariahs, multiple Jonathans. On that logic, one Libni is Gershonite and the other is Merarite, end of story. That move is available and we should take it seriously. But here's the textual problem. Look at 1 Chronicles 6 as a literary unit. The chapter is systematically listing Levi's descendants by branch. Verses 16-19 lay out the three Levitical branches (Gershon, Kohath, Merari) and verse 17 explicitly identifies Libni as Gershon's son. Then verse 29, in the SAME chapter, reassigns Libni to the Merari line. Knoppers in his AB commentary on 1 Chronicles flags this as a likely corruption or textual transmission error — the parallel list in Merari's line should probably read a different name, and the LXX tradition preserves some variation. The apologist "two different Libnis" defense requires that the Chronicler, writing a unified genealogical treatise, inserted two identically-named figures in two different branches without comment. That's possible. It's also the least parsimonious reading. The simpler explanation is textual corruption in the Masoretic tradition, which is what Noth, Japhet, and Knoppers all argue. Either way, as the text stands the two verses contradict each other.

entries.question: How many days is unleavened bread to be eaten during the Passover?
entries.summary: Exodus 12:15, 13:6-7, 23:15, Leviticus 23:6, and Deuteronomy 16:3 all require seven days of unleavened bread. But Deuteronomy 16:8, three verses after Deut 16:3 says seven, specifies six days of unleavened bread followed by a solemn assembly on the seventh. Even internally within Deuteronomy 16, the count flips between six and seven.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is mathematically creative. Keil-Delitzsch and Craigie both try versions of it. The argument: Deut 16:3 says seven days, Deut 16:8 says six days, and the reconciliation is that the seventh day is a "solemn assembly" (atzeret) on which you ALSO eat unleavened bread, just in a different liturgical frame, so the total is still seven days of unleavened bread with six ordinary days plus one sacred assembly day. That actually could work grammatically if you're willing to read "six days" as "six ordinary days" with the seventh being counted separately. Tigay takes this line in his JPS Torah Commentary on Deuteronomy. But here's the textual problem. The Exodus and Leviticus texts never split the count. They say "seven days" cleanly. Only Deuteronomy 16:8 introduces "six days" language. Levinson and Bernard Levinson specifically (different scholars, same surname — I mean Bernard M. Levinson, the Deuteronomy/hermeneutics guy) argues in Deuteronomy and the Hermeneutics of Legal Innovation that Deuteronomy is deliberately reworking the older festival calendar — combining Pesach with Chag Matzot and centralizing the festival at the chosen place. The six-day count in Deut 16:8 is a vestige of that redactional reworking. So the apologist can technically reconcile the numbers by reading the seventh day as a separate category, but that reading requires accepting that Deuteronomy has a different festival structure than Exodus-Leviticus — which is exactly what critical scholars are saying when they call this a contradiction. Harmonization and source criticism are pointing at the same thing; only the framing differs.

entries.question: Did God kill all the Egyptian cattle in the sixth plague?
entries.summary: Exodus 9:3-6 (the fifth plague, the murrain — the question's "sixth" is wrong) says "all the cattle of Egypt died." Three verses later at Exodus 9:19, God is warning Egyptians to bring their cattle and servants indoors because hail is coming and what's left in the field will die. So either "all" didn't mean all, or there's a narrative continuity problem between the fifth and seventh plagues.
entries.commentary: The apologist standard move on this one is the "all" hyperbole defense. Archer, Stuart, and Kaiser all run it. The argument: biblical Hebrew routinely uses kol ("all") hyperbolically — think of "all the world went out to be taxed" in Luke 2:1, or "all Judea went out to John the Baptist." On this reading, "all the cattle of Egypt died" means "all the cattle that were in the field as specified in Exodus 9:3" — the murrain only struck field cattle, not sheltered cattle, so there are cattle left for Exodus 9:19's hail plague. Keil-Delitzsch formulated this harmonization and every conservative commentary since has leaned on it. Here's where it gets interesting. Exodus 9:3 does in fact specify that the murrain is "upon thy cattle which is in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep." So the harmonization isn't invented from thin air — it's scaffolded on the actual text. BUT. Exodus 9:6 explicitly says "all the cattle of Egypt died" without repeating the "in the field" qualifier, and then 9:7 says Pharaoh sent messengers and found "there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead." The contrast is between all-dead-Egyptian and all-alive-Israelite, which is how the plague gets its rhetorical punch. Propp in the Anchor Bible commentary on Exodus notes the tension and suggests the plagues are composite — the "all cattle died" is from one stratum and the hail's cattle survivors are from another, stitched together by the redactor without smoothing out the death count. Friedman assigns the murrain primarily to E and the hail primarily to J, which helps explain why the cattle count doesn't add up across plagues. The apologist hyperbole defense works if you're willing to let "all" mean "some" whenever the narrative gets trapped, but then "all the cattle died" is just a rhetorical flourish, not an actual datum about what happened. Flag: the question text incorrectly calls this the sixth plague — it's the fifth (murrain). The sixth plague is boils (Exod 9:8-12).

entries.question: Is God warlike or peaceful?
entries.books_in_tension: Exodus, Psalms, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, 2 Thessalonians, Hebrews
entries.summary: Exodus 15:3 calls YHWH "a man of war" and Psalms 18:34 and 144:1 describe YHWH as the one who teaches hands to war and fingers to fight. The New Testament, by contrast, repeatedly titles God "the God of peace" (Rom 15:33, 16:20, 2 Cor 13:11, 1 Thess 5:23, Heb 13:20) and declares God is "not the author of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33). The contradiction is between a martial YHWH who trains warriors and a peaceful God who authors shalom.
entries.commentary: This is a category the apologist usually wins the surface skirmish on and loses the deep argument. The surface move is easy: God is both. He is peaceful toward his people and warlike toward his enemies. War and peace aren't contradictory attributes; they're contextual expressions of righteousness. Copan runs this line in Is God a Moral Monster?, Wright in The God I Don't Understand, and Longman in Reading the Bible with Heart and Mind. Fine. That move has textual support — there's plenty of material in both Testaments where God's peace toward Israel requires martial action against Israel's enemies. Psalm 46 has "he maketh wars to cease" as proof of divine peace. Here's where the critical scholarship lands. Mark S. Smith in The Early History of God documents that early Israelite YHWH was indistinguishable from Canaanite and Mesopotamian warrior gods — the divine warrior motif ("man of war" — ish milkhamah) is stock ANE storm-god imagery, closely paralleled by Baal, Marduk, Ashur. Patrick D. Miller in The Divine Warrior in Early Israel catalogs how deeply this warlike portrayal saturates pre-exilic material. The shift to "God of peace" framing in the New Testament is not a contradiction in the apologist's sense; it's a theological development across centuries, as Israelite religion moved through the exile, the Hellenistic period, and emergent Christianity, progressively reframing God's character. Jon Levenson covers this in Creation and the Persistence of Evil. So the apologist harmonization "he's peaceful to his people and warlike to enemies" flattens a real theological evolution into a single timeless attribute. The text DOES present two different models of God — one from Bronze Age divine-warrior theology, the other from a later peace theology. The apologist is reading both through a single systematic-theology filter. Critical scholarship reads them as evidence of genuine theological development over time.

entries.question: Is dancing a sin?
entries.summary: Exodus 32:19-28 has Moses kill 3,000 Israelites after catching them dancing around the golden calf, treating the dancing as part of the capital offense. Exodus 15:20-21, just seventeen chapters earlier, has Miriam and the women dancing with timbrels to celebrate YHWH's defeat of Pharaoh's army — treated as praise, not sin. Same book, dancing gets you killed in chapter 32 and praised in chapter 15.
entries.commentary: This is a weak contradiction on its face and the apologist is right to push back. Dancing is not intrinsically sinful in biblical thought — it's how the dancing is directed that matters. Miriam's dance in Exodus 15 is praise to YHWH after the Red Sea crossing. The golden calf dance in Exodus 32 is idolatrous worship of a forbidden image. 2 Samuel 6 has David dancing before the ark as worship. Ecclesiastes 3:4 has "a time to dance." Psalm 149:3 and 150:4 commend dancing as praise. So on the context-matters framing, the contradiction dissolves — and that's what Archer, Mathews, and Kaiser argue. I don't think the apologist is wrong on this one. What's actually being punished in Exodus 32 is the worship of the calf, which was the breach of the first and second commandments. The dancing is incidental coloring of the idolatrous scene, not the offense itself. The text supports that reading — Moses' anger in 32:19-20 is directed at the calf, not at the dancing per se. Fretheim, Propp, and Sarna (JPS Exodus commentary) all read the dance as part of the idolatrous cultic scene rather than as the sin-in-itself. That said, the SAB framing isn't entirely empty — it does capture a surface-level oddity: the same physical act (group dance with musical instruments) triggers opposite narrative valences in the same book, and the distinction between "sacred dance" and "idolatrous dance" is nowhere explicitly defined by the text. A naive reader getting the Ten Commandments as their filter might reasonably wonder what the difference is. But as contradictions go, this is low-grade. The verdict: context-sensitive ritual categories are doing the work, and the text is internally coherent once you read the cult context. Flagging as a weak contradiction without recommending delete.

entries.question: What was in the Ark of the Covenant?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 8:9 and 2 Chronicles 5:10 both state flatly that when Solomon brought the ark into the temple, "there was nothing in the ark save the two tables of stone." Hebrews 9:4, describing the same ark, says it contained "the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant" — three items, not one. Either the ark had three things in it or it had only one. The two texts contradict.
entries.commentary: This is a hard one for apologists and the standard harmonization shows the strain. Archer, Ellingworth (NIGTC Hebrews), and Lane (WBC Hebrews) all try variants of the same move: at the original construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 16:33-34 for the manna jar, Numbers 17:10 for Aaron's rod), those items were placed "before the Testimony" or "before the ark" — which may have meant beside or in front of rather than strictly inside. The apologist argument is that Hebrews 9:4 is using "in" loosely to mean "associated with the ark," and that by Solomon's time the pot and rod had been removed, so 1 Kings 8:9 is historically accurate for Solomon's era. That is a multi-layer rescue. It requires (1) Hebrews using a preposition loosely, (2) a tradition about items being associated-but-not-inside, and (3) an undocumented removal of items between the wilderness and Solomon's temple. Attridge in his Hermeneia commentary on Hebrews reads the text straightforwardly — the Greek en he ("in which") means what it says: the author of Hebrews is describing the ark as containing all three items. Attridge notes that the author is drawing on a priestly-traditional picture of the ark, not on actual Solomonic practice, and that there is a genuine inconsistency with 1 Kings / 2 Chronicles. Koester (AB Hebrews) and deSilva (Perseverance in Gratitude) come to similar conclusions. The Numbers 17 and Exodus 16 texts specifically say the manna jar and Aaron's rod were placed "before the Testimony" — which in context is language for being in the most holy place, near the ark, but the author of Hebrews has apparently conflated that with being inside the ark. The apologist's loose-preposition defense is technically possible but it's post-hoc rationalization. The parsimonious reading is that Hebrews, writing in the late first century to a Diaspora audience, drew on an extracanonical or liturgical tradition about the ark's contents that differed from the Kings/Chronicles historical record. Two traditions, stitched together, don't match.

entries.question: Where did Moses get water from a rock?
entries.summary: Exodus 17:1-7 locates the water-from-rock miracle at Rephidim in the wilderness of Sin ("the rock in Horeb"), with Moses naming the place Massah and Meribah. Numbers 20:1-8 (with Num 27:14 and Deut 32:51 confirming) locates it at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, at the waters of "Meribah-Kadesh." Two different wildernesses, two different locations, same miracle (or so it appears).
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization on this one is clean and well-established: there are two separate water-from-rock miracles. Archer, Kaiser, and Ashley (NICOT Numbers) all make this move. The evidence supports it. Exodus 17 happens early in the wilderness wanderings, shortly after the Red Sea crossing, at Rephidim. Numbers 20 happens in the fortieth year, at Kadesh, where Miriam has just died and where Moses will be punished for striking the rock instead of speaking to it. Different locations, different timeframes, different outcomes (Moses is faithful in Exodus 17, disobedient in Numbers 20). On the surface, this resolves the contradiction: the two stories are two distinct events with the coincidental shared name "Meribah" attached because both involved water disputes. That is a reasonable reading and in harmonization terms, it works. But the critical scholarly read complicates it. Budd in his WBC commentary on Numbers, Levine in the AB commentary, and Friedman in The Bible with Sources Revealed all argue that Exodus 17 (JE) and Numbers 20 (P) are variant traditions of the same underlying event, redactionally separated and placed at different points in the wilderness narrative. The clues: both miracles are named Meribah (strife), both involve a rock being struck, both involve water for a rebellious congregation, and the Deuteronomy 33:8 blessing of Levi refers to a SINGLE event ("thou didst prove at Massah, and... at the waters of Meribah"). The most parsimonious source-critical reading is that P retold the J/E Rephidim story to relocate it to Kadesh and to add Moses' disobedience as the etiological explanation for why Moses wouldn't enter the promised land. So the apologist "two separate miracles" defense reconciles the surface contradiction at the cost of ignoring the structural parallels that suggest one underlying tradition doubled by the redactor. Both readings are defensible, but the critical one has stronger source-critical warrants.

entries.question: Can God be tempted?
entries.summary: James 1:13 declares God "cannot be tempted with evil" — a flat denial of divine temptability. Deuteronomy 6:16 (and Jesus citing it at Matt 4:7 / Luke 4:12) commands "Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God" — a command that presupposes God CAN be tempted, otherwise why forbid it? The verses contradict on whether God is subject to temptation at all.
entries.commentary: This one actually turns on a translation and semantic range problem, and the apologist is partially right. The Greek peirazo and Hebrew nasah cover a semantic range from "tempt (to sin)" to "test" to "put to the proof." James 1:13 uses peirazo in the moral-solicitation sense — God cannot be seduced into evil. Deuteronomy 6:16 and Jesus' citation of it use the same verb family but in a different sense: don't put God on trial, don't demand that God prove himself, don't treat God like a subject of experiment. Blomberg and Carson run this argument and they're not wrong about the semantic difference. So in English the word "tempt" looks like the same concept, but the underlying Hebrew and Greek are deploying different senses. The harmonization wins the surface skirmish. Here's where it gets interesting. Even granting the semantic distinction, the theological problem doesn't fully disappear. James 1:13 isn't just saying "God can't be morally solicited," it's making a broader claim about divine impassibility — that God is not subject to internal disruption by external stimuli. But the Hebrew Bible has YHWH regularly being "tested" by Israel (Exod 17:2, Num 14:22, Ps 78:18, 41, 56, 95:9) and responding with anger, disappointment, and changed plans. That's not temptation-to-sin, but it IS being moved by external provocation, which is in tension with James' absolute framing. Kugel notes in How to Read the Bible that the Hebrew Bible's God is profoundly responsive — he grieves (Gen 6:6), relents (Exod 32:14, Jonah 3:10), and changes his mind (1 Sam 15:11). The James 1:13 framing reflects a later Hellenistic-Jewish and early Christian theology of divine impassibility, influenced by Greek philosophical categories, that is at tension with older Hebraic portrayals. So while the narrow "tempt = solicit to evil" harmonization works for the lexical contradiction, there's a deeper theological tension between the two portrayals of divine susceptibility. The SAB is raising a real issue even if the specific verse pairing is semantically sloppy.

entries.question: How did God tell Moses to get water from a rock?
entries.summary: Exodus 17:5-7 has God instructing Moses to strike (smite) the rock with his rod. Numbers 20:7-8 has God instructing Moses to SPEAK to the rock — and the whole point of Numbers 20's narrative is that Moses' striking (instead of speaking) is the transgression that bars him from the promised land. Deuteronomy 33:8 adds a third element: the Urim and Thummim (mistyped in the scrape as "Umim and Thumim") "proved" Moses at Massah and Meribah, hinting at a divinatory element in the tradition. The three texts describe three different divine instructions for the same category of miracle.
entries.commentary: This is a structurally richer version of contradiction 111, and the harmonization moves are similar but the stakes are higher because the method matters for the narrative. The apologist move is the same two-miracles defense: Exodus 17 is one event where striking was commanded; Numbers 20 is a second event forty years later where speaking was commanded and Moses disobeyed by striking anyway. Archer runs this straightforwardly. Deuteronomy 33:8's Urim-and-Thummim reference is a Mosaic blessing on Levi that poetically references the Massah/Meribah events without explicitly specifying a divinatory method for producing water — the apologist reads it as referring to Levi's priestly role having been validated at these events, not as a separate method for water production. Craigie, Merrill (NAC), and Tigay (JPS) all handle it this way. That's a reasonable reading of Deut 33:8. Where the apologist defense strains is Numbers 20 itself. Granted the two-miracles framing, the critical reader still has to reckon with the source-critical evidence that Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 are doublets from different sources — Friedman, Baden, Budd, and Levine all make this case. The repetition of Meribah, the near-identical plot structure, the water shortage, the rock, the rod — these are literary parallels too close to be coincidental. Milgrom in his JPS Numbers commentary explicitly argues Numbers 20 is P's retelling of the older JE Rephidim tradition, relocated to Kadesh and modified to include Moses' disqualifying sin (striking instead of speaking). So the methodology disagreement between Exodus 17 (strike) and Numbers 20 (speak) isn't evidence of two separate events where Moses got different instructions — it's evidence that the P author deliberately reframed the JE striking-miracle as a disobedience narrative to explain Moses' exclusion from the land. The Deuteronomy 33:8 allusion to Massah/Meribah isn't a third method; it's a Deuteronomic echo of the older tradition. Three variant traditions, one underlying event, different theological purposes.

entries.question: Who was Moses' father-in-law?
entries.summary: Three different names are given for Moses' father-in-law. Exodus 3:1, 4:18, 18:1, 18:5 all call him Jethro (the priest of Midian). Numbers 10:29 and Judges 4:11 call him Hobab. Exodus 2:18-21 calls him Reuel. The verses directly identify different men by different names in the same narrative role.
entries.commentary: This is one of the classic Pentateuch contradictions, and the apologist moves are creative but strained. Archer, Kaiser, and Cole (TOTC Exodus) all run versions of two reconciliation strategies. Strategy one: Reuel is the clan-name or grandfather, Jethro is the given name, Hobab is a separate individual (Moses' brother-in-law, not father-in-law). The Numbers 10:29 reference to "Hobab, the son of Raguel" (Raguel being Reuel) is then read as Moses addressing his brother-in-law — Hobab — calling Reuel the father-in-law. Strategy two: the same man had multiple names, as was common in the ANE — Reuel was his given name, Jethro ("excellency") was his priestly title, Hobab was a nickname or additional name. That harmonization is not zero. ANE figures did often have multiple names — think Abram/Abraham, Jacob/Israel, Gideon/Jerubbaal. And the Hebrew word translated "father in law" (חֹתֵן, choten) can mean broader in-law relation, including brother-in-law. So the apologist defense is available. Here's the source-critical reading. Propp in the AB Exodus commentary and Friedman in Who Wrote the Bible argue that the J source uses Reuel (Exod 2:18), the E source uses Jethro (Exod 3:1, 4:18, 18), and Numbers 10:29 (also J in Friedman's analysis) uses "Hobab son of Reuel." Judges 4:11, which has Hobab as father-in-law, is a separate tradition, likely deuteronomistic, that diverges from the Pentateuchal accounts. The simplest reading: multiple sources had different names for Moses' father-in-law, reflecting different oral traditions about this peripheral Midianite figure, and the redactor harmonized them incompletely. The apologist "three names for one man" defense is possible but requires a complex reading of choten in Numbers 10:29 and an unexplained why-would-he-have-three-names scenario. The source-critical explanation is parsimonious. Take your pick.

entries.question: Is it OK to make images?
entries.summary: The Second Commandment in Exodus 20:4 and Deuteronomy 5:8 prohibits making "any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath." Deuteronomy 4:16-18, 4:23, and 27:15 reinforce this as an absolute ban. But Exodus 25:18-20 has God himself commanding Moses to make two gold cherubim (winged images of heavenly beings) to cover the mercy seat, and Exodus 26:1 adds cherubim woven into the tabernacle curtains. God forbids images of heavenly beings and simultaneously commands images of heavenly beings.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is elegant and partially works. The argument, run by Archer, Mathews, Sarna (JPS Exodus), and Propp: the prohibition in Exodus 20:4 is not against image-making per se but against image-making for worship (the next clause, 20:5, is "thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them"). Cherubim on the mercy seat and woven into curtains are images — but they're not worshipped. They're decorative or theologically functional, not cultic objects of devotion. On this reading, the commandment is about idolatry, not about iconography. This is a solid reading and the apologist has internal biblical warrant for it. The bronze serpent in Numbers 21:8-9 fits the same pattern — God commands a serpent image for healing purposes; Hezekiah later destroys it (2 Kings 18:4) precisely because people started worshipping it. Solomon's temple had cherubim, lions, oxen, and pomegranates as decorative elements (1 Kings 7) without apparent violation. So the apologist is right that the Second Commandment is about cultic use, not image-making as such. Where it gets interesting is that this interpretation is not unanimous within the biblical tradition. The strictest deuteronomic strand (Deut 4:16-18 especially) reads like a near-absolute ban on any likenesses of creatures, and second-temple Judaism inherited this more rigorous reading — leading to the aniconic coin tradition under the Hasmoneans, the destruction of the Roman eagle over the temple under Herod, and the eventual rabbinic discomfort with figural art (though the Dura-Europos synagogue in the 3rd century CE shows the rule wasn't absolute even then). Moberly in Old Testament Theology and Halbertal-Margalit in Idolatry both note that the Hebrew Bible contains at least two distinct iconic theologies: a cherubim-are-fine strand (P, priestly) and a no-images-at-all strand (strict Deuteronomic). The apologist "it's about worship, not making" reading is the P-strand reading. It works for resolving Exodus 20 vs Exodus 25, but it glosses over the genuine tension between the priestly iconic tradition and the stricter deuteronomic anti-iconic tradition. The biblical text contains both theological strands, and the SAB contradiction is pointing at that internal diversity even if clumsily.

entries.question: How should parents be treated?
entries.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Matthew, Luke, John, Ephesians
entries.summary: The Torah and the wisdom literature hand down an unambiguous rule: honor your father and mother. It is one of the Ten Commandments, repeated in Deuteronomy, echoed in Proverbs, and reaffirmed by Paul as "the first commandment with promise." Then the Gospels put words in Jesus' mouth that run the other way — disciples must "hate" father and mother, leave a father unburied, and call no man on earth their father. One stream demands you honor your parents; the other demands you subordinate or reject them for the sake of the kingdom. They cannot both be the operative standard at the same time.
entries.commentary:
Here's the thing — the honor side isn't ambiguous. Exodus 20:12 makes parental honor a Decalogue obligation, Deuteronomy 5:16 attaches a long-life reward to it, and Ephesians 6:2 calls it "the first commandment with promise." That's the baseline the Gospel sayings collide with.

Apologists have three main escape routes, and the strongest version of each deserves a fair hearing. First, the Semitic-idiom move: the Greek μισέω (miseo, "hate") in Luke 14:26 renders a Hebrew idiom of preference, so "hate" just means "love less." Genesis 29:31 (Leah "hated") and the Matthew 10:37 parallel ("loveth father or mother more than me") give that reading real support. Second, the life-stages move: honor binds you as a child, while the discipleship sayings address adults choosing a vocation — different situations, no conflict. Third, the radicalizing move: Jesus isn't abolishing the commandment, he's relativizing all earthly loyalties under the kingdom, the way Mark 7:9-13 actually defends parental support against the corban dodge.

The idiom argument is the best of the bunch — Matthew clearly softened Luke's wording for exactly this reason, which tells you the early church already felt the friction. But softening "hate" to "love less" doesn't dissolve the problem; it relocates it. A commandment that says honor your parents is hard to square with a teacher who makes loving them less than him the entry ticket to discipleship. And Luke 9:59-60 won't bend to the idiom defense at all: refusing to let a man bury his own father isn't "loving him less," it's overriding one of the most sacred filial duties in Second Temple Judaism. The harmonizations require you to read each hard saying through the softest available lens while ignoring that the texts themselves are pulling in opposite directions. The tension is real, and the church's own editorial fingerprints prove it felt real to them too.

entries.question: Is it wrong to have sex outside of marriage?
entries.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Hosea, Acts, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, Hebrews, Jude
entries.summary: The Torah (Exod 20:14, Deut 5:18) and the New Testament (Acts 15:20, 1 Cor 5:1, 6:13, 6:18, 10:8, 2 Cor 12:21, Gal 5:19-21, Eph 5:3, Col 3:5-6, 1 Thess 4:3, Heb 13:4, Jude 7) repeatedly condemn fornication and adultery. But Hosea 1:2 and 3:1 have YHWH commanding the prophet Hosea to take a "wife of whoredoms" and later to love an adulteress — God explicitly commanding the act his own law forbids.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here is clean and widely held: Hosea 1 and 3 are prophetic symbolic actions, not endorsements of fornication. The marriage of Hosea to Gomer is a divinely commanded object lesson about Israel's infidelity to YHWH, not a general license for sexual immorality. Stuart (WBC Hosea), Garrett (NAC Hosea), and Dearman (NICOT Hosea) all take this line. The apologist argument: Hosea's marriage operates in a special category of prophetic sign-act, parallel to Ezekiel lying on his side for 390 days, Isaiah walking naked for three years, or Jeremiah wearing a yoke — these are symbolic acts that would be problematic if done for their own sake but are meaningful as embodied prophecy. On this reading, Hosea is not committing adultery himself; he is MARRYING a woman with an immoral past or promiscuous character as a living metaphor for YHWH's covenant with unfaithful Israel. That harmonization works. The sign-act genre is well-documented in ANE prophetic literature, and the context of Hosea makes the symbolic purpose explicit. Andersen and Freedman's AB commentary lays this out exhaustively. Here's where it gets complicated. Even granting the sign-act reading, the contradiction doesn't fully dissolve. The command in Hosea 1:2 isn't "marry a woman who WAS promiscuous and is now repentant" — it's "take a wife of whoredoms AND children of whoredoms, for the land hath committed great whoredom." Hosea 3:1 explicitly commands love for an adulteress, and the prophet pays silver and barley as if purchasing her (3:2). The moral category of the act is messy. Hebrew Bible scholars like Heschel (The Prophets) and Brueggemann (Prophetic Imagination) point out that the prophetic sign-acts DO involve the prophet in morally complex behavior that stretches or contravenes normal ethical categories — that's part of their rhetorical force. So the apologist is right that it's not a simple endorsement of fornication, but the contradiction is real at the level of divine command: God is commanding behavior that his law elsewhere condemns, and he's doing so for a higher pedagogical purpose. The SAB framing is a bit blunt but the underlying tension is genuine. This is a case where "God is above his own law when he has a reason" is the actual apologist answer, which is itself a theologically interesting concession.

entries.question: Is it OK to covet?
entries.summary: The Tenth Commandment as quoted by Paul in Romans 7:7 and 13:9 prohibits coveting, and Ephesians 5:3 and Colossians 3:5 reinforce that covetousness is idolatry and should not even be named among believers. But 1 Corinthians 14:39 has Paul himself saying "covet to prophesy" — using the same Greek verb (zeloo, in some manuscripts; KJV renders zelote as "covet") in a positive sense. Paul is simultaneously condemning covetousness and commanding it.
entries.commentary: This is a translation contradiction, and the apologist is right on it. The KJV "covet to prophesy" is translating zeloute (from zeloo, to be zealous, to strive after, to earnestly desire) — the SAME root that gives us "jealous" and "zealot." The prohibitions on coveting in Romans 7:7 and 13:9 translate the Greek epithymeo (to desire, lust after) — a different verb. Ephesians 5:3 and Colossians 3:5 use pleonexia (greed, grasping for more) — also a different word. Three different Greek words all rendered "covet" in the KJV because Jacobean English had a narrower vocabulary. Modern translations handle this cleanly: ESV has "earnestly desire" for 1 Cor 14:39, "covet" for the prohibitions. NIV has "eagerly desire" for 1 Cor 14:39. This is a pure translation artifact, not a substantive contradiction. Archer notes this correctly, and Fee (NICNT 1 Corinthians) and Thiselton (NIGTC) both handle the Greek precisely. The contradiction only exists in the KJV and in readers who don't check the underlying Greek. That said, the SAB is using a King James-centric framing that wouldn't register the contradiction in any modern translation. If the question is "is there a genuine contradiction in the New Testament Greek," the answer is no. If the question is "does the KJV contradict itself with the same English word," the answer is yes, but that's a translation issue, not a textual one. Flag: this is a weak contradiction that dissolves under minimal exegesis. The underlying Greek distinguishes what the English conflates. Verdict: the text does not contradict itself; the translation does.

entries.question: Who gave the law to Moses?
entries.summary: The Exodus narrative (Exod 19:20, 20:22) has YHWH descending on Sinai and speaking the law directly to Moses — no intermediaries. But Galatians 3:19 explicitly says the law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator" — Paul is telling his Gentile converts that the Torah came through angels and a human mediator (Moses), not directly from God. Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2 echo the angel-mediation tradition. Two different models of Sinai revelation.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization here actually has solid second-temple texture behind it, but it still leaves the contradiction largely intact. The argument: Exodus 19-20 says God descended on Sinai and spoke with Moses, but it doesn't explicitly deny angelic involvement. Second-temple Jewish tradition — Jubilees, Philo, Josephus, and the LXX translation of Deut 33:2 — developed a theology in which angels were present at Sinai and served as intermediaries in the law's transmission. Paul is drawing on this established tradition, not inventing it. Bruce (NICNT Galatians), Longenecker (WBC Galatians), and Moo (BECNT Galatians) all make this point, and Dunn's Galatians commentary goes further. On this reading, Galatians 3:19 isn't contradicting Exodus; it's drawing on a Jewish interpretive tradition that filled in Sinai with angelic mediators. That IS historically accurate. Philo's De Somniis and Josephus's Antiquities 15.136 both reference angelic involvement at Sinai. The LXX of Deuteronomy 33:2 reads "at his right hand were angels" where the Hebrew has "from his right hand was a fiery law." So Paul is working within an existing interpretive framework. Here's where the critical read lands. The Exodus narrative itself, in its plain reading, does NOT include angelic mediators. YHWH speaks, Moses hears, the people tremble and refuse direct revelation (20:18-21), and Moses becomes the mediator. But the mediator in Exodus is Moses, not angels plus Moses. The angelic-mediator tradition is a second-temple development, not an exegetical entailment of the Pentateuchal text. Paul in Galatians 3 is using this tradition for a specific polemical purpose — he's diminishing the Torah's ontological status to make room for Christ as a superior mediator. The more direct the law's origin, the harder for Paul to relativize it; the more layers of mediation (angels, then human mediator), the easier. Martyn in the AB Galatians commentary argues Paul is deliberately minimizing the law's divine directness. So Paul isn't just reporting a tradition; he's weaponizing it theologically. The contradiction between Exodus and Galatians is real, and the second-temple angelic-mediation tradition is interesting context but doesn't erase the difference in how Sinai is described.
